title: Willie Mosconi and the 526-Ball Run: The Story Behind the Mosconi Cup Name
desc: Who was Willie Mosconi? His 19 world straight pool titles, the 526-ball run in 1954, The Hustler, and how his record was finally broken.
body:
In two weeks, the best players in America and Europe will fight over a trophy named after him at the 2026 Mosconi Cup in Orlando. But plenty of fans who chant through those matches couldn't tell you much about Willie Mosconi himself. Here is the story of the man pool players called "Mr. Pocket Billiards," and the 526-ball run that made his name a measuring stick for 65 years.

A kid who wasn't supposed to play

William Joseph Mosconi was born in Philadelphia on June 27, 1913. His family lived above a pool hall his father ran, and you would think that meant a head start. It didn't, at least not at first. According to Wikipedia's biography, his father didn't want Willie playing and hid the balls, so the boy practiced with a broomstick and small potatoes on the table.

The talent showed early anyway. At six, he played an exhibition against the reigning world champion, Ralph Greenleaf, and lost. By 11 he was a juvenile straight pool champion. In 1933, after a strong showing at a national championship, Brunswick hired him and sent him on tour with Greenleaf, the very player who had beaten him as a little kid.

Nineteen world titles

Mosconi's game was straight pool (14.1 continuous), where you call every shot, score one point per ball, and keep shooting as long as you don't miss. When 14 balls are down, they get re-racked and you break into the pack while running the 15th ball. It is a game of pure control, and nobody controlled it like Mosconi.

He won the World Straight Pool Championship 19 times, starting in 1941 and running into the mid-1950s. He took a break from competition to serve in the U.S. Army in 1944, and a stroke in 1956 slowed him down. Still, he kept playing at a high level and won the National Invitational in 1958. He finally retired from tournament play in 1966.

The 526-ball run

The record that defines him happened on March 19, 1954, at the East High Billiard Club in Springfield, Ohio. According to the pool history site PoolHistory.com, Mosconi was playing an exhibition of 14.1 against a local player named Earl "Jake" Bruney. After he won the match, he kept shooting, and shooting, and shooting.

About four and a half hours later he had pocketed 526 balls in a row. That's more than 37 full racks without a miss.

A few details make the number even more impressive:

  • It was an exhibition, in front of a crowd. Wikipedia notes the run is backed by a notarized affidavit signed by more than 35 eyewitnesses.
  • The table was not small. PoolHistory.com describes it as an oversized 4x8-foot Brunswick table.
  • It lasted. Nobody officially topped it for 65 years.

Mosconi had other huge runs too. Wikipedia lists runs of 322, 355 and 365 in 1953 alone. But 526 became the number every straight pool player knew by heart.

When the record finally fell

On May 27, 2019, John Schmidt ran 626 balls at Easy Street Billiards in Monterey, California, in an exhibition set up specifically to chase the record. According to PoolHistory.com, the Billiard Congress of America reviewed the unedited video and recognized it as the new 14.1 exhibition high run record in August 2019.

In 2022, Jayson Shaw went further. AZBilliards reported his run of 714, and after review it was recognized as 669, because of a ball he touched early in the run.

Some old-school fans still argue that Mosconi's 526 deserves its own category, since he did it during a match and on a table that wasn't set up for a record attempt. That is a fun barroom debate, and there is no wrong answer. What isn't up for debate is that it took more than six decades, and modern equipment and video, for anybody to pass him.

The Hustler and the TV era

Mosconi's influence spread way past the pool room. For the 1961 film The Hustler, he was the technical adviser. According to Wikipedia, he taught Paul Newman how to walk, talk and shoot like a pool player, and he recommended Jackie Gleason for the role of Minnesota Fats. He even has a small cameo in the movie. It is still one of the best pool movies ever made, and the boom in pool rooms after its release is part of pool history.

Later, he played televised exhibition matches, including a famous 1978 "Great Pool Shoot-Out" against Rudolf Wanderone, the real-life player who called himself Minnesota Fats. Wikipedia records Mosconi winning all three games they played that day: 9-Ball, 8-Ball and rotation.

He also wrote. His instruction book Willie Mosconi on Pocket Billiards came out in 1948, and his autobiography, Willie's Game, was published in 1993. The Billiard Congress of America inducted him into its Hall of Fame in 1968.

Mosconi died on September 17, 1993, at 80. The first Mosconi Cup was held the next year, in 1994.

What weekend players can learn from Mosconi

You don't need to run 526 to steal from his game. A few things Mosconi was known for apply to anyone who plays in a weekly tournament:

  • Short, simple position. Straight pool rewards keeping the cue ball in the middle of the table with small, controlled moves. Fewer rails, fewer surprises. Our position play guide breaks this down.
  • Play the stop shot and stun. Most long runs are built on cue ball moves of a foot or two. Practice them with our stop shot and stun shot guide.
  • Keep a rhythm. Long runs come from a steady, repeatable routine on every shot. Build one with our pre-shot routine guide.
  • Practice straight pool even if you play 9-Ball. A simple goal like running 10, then 15, then 20 balls is one of the best practice drills there is.

Watch his name in action

When the Mosconi Cup starts on November 27, every match is played in his honor. Catch up on the latest from the pro game in our pool news roundup, and dig into the bigger picture with our history of pool.

Then go make some history of your own. Find a pool tournament near you this weekend, or browse upcoming tournaments by state.

faq: What was Willie Mosconi's high run?
526 consecutive balls in straight pool (14.1), made on March 19, 1954, during an exhibition at the East High Billiard Club in Springfield, Ohio.
How many world titles did Willie Mosconi win?
He won the World Straight Pool Championship 19 times, starting in 1941.
John Schmidt ran 626 in 2019, recognized by the Billiard Congress of America. Jayson Shaw later ran a reported 714 in 2022, recognized as 669 after review.
Why is the Mosconi Cup named after him?
The USA vs. Europe 9-Ball event was created in 1994, the year after his death, and named in honor of the American straight pool legend.
